h1: The 6 Best OLED TVs of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six OLED TVs from LG and Samsung, from 42 to 77 inches, sorted by room size, series and who each set is best for.
summary: The LG 65 inch C6 OLED evo is the best OLED TV here, pairing the newer series with the most popular size and a clearer listing. The Samsung S90H at 65 inches is the cross-brand alternative. The LG C5 in 55 inches is the value route, and the 42 inch C6 is the only compact set.
intro: The most common OLED shopping mistake is comparing by brand and skipping the series year. An LG C5 and a C6 look alike on a showroom shelf, yet the lettered line and the number after it tell you which generation you are buying, and the newer one is the benchmark every other set should be measured against. Price gaps between years can be real, so decide whether the difference matters before you decide on size.

We reviewed eight listings and ranked six on series, size, platform and price bucket. The listings mostly give size, panel type and Dolby Atmos support, so we rank on those and avoid claims about brightness or motion handling that we cannot back. Treat the ranking as a guide to what each listing proves, then verify the rest.

products.name: LG 65-Inch Class OLED evo AI 4K C6 Series Smart TV w/Dolby Atmos
products.verdict: The current C6 series in the most popular size, with Dolby Atmos.
products.description:
The LG 65 inch C6 is an OLED evo with AI features, 4K resolution and Dolby Atmos support, in the $500 and up bucket. OLED lights each pixel individually, so black areas can switch fully off, which is why OLED is the reference for dark-room viewing. Sixty-five inches is the size where a living room's seating distance and wall width usually line up.

It leads because it combines the newer C6 series with the most popular size and a more detailed listing than the Samsung. The S90H competes at the same size, but states less.

Buy it for a main living room. The caveat is that the listing says little about brightness, which matters if your room gets strong daylight. It also sits in the premium bucket, so skip it if you want the lowest price.

products.name: Samsung 65-Inch Class S90H Series
products.verdict: Samsung's S90H OLED at 65 inches, the cross-brand alternative.
products.description:
The Samsung S90H in 65 inches is an OLED set in the $500 and up bucket. The listing is brief, naming the series, size and panel type, which makes it hard to compare against LG on anything but those three facts.

It ranks second because the LG listing gives more detail, including the Dolby Atmos support, and the C6 is the newer-looking series in this list. The two brands compete at the same size, so the choice between them often comes down to interface and ecosystem. If you already use Samsung phones, tablets or a SmartThings setup, the S90H fits naturally.

Buy it if you prefer Samsung's interface. Skip it if you want a detailed spec sheet before committing. Check ports and refresh rate on the manufacturer page, since the listing here omits them.
products.skipIf: You want a detailed spec sheet.

products.name: LG 55-Inch Class OLED evo AI 4K C5 Series Smart TV w/Dolby Atmos
products.verdict: The previous-generation C5 in 55 inches, often the value route.
products.description:
The LG C5 in 55 inches is an OLED evo 4K set with AI features and Dolby Atmos, in the $500 and up bucket. It is the previous-generation series, which is where the value argument lives: when a new series arrives, the old one often drops in price while keeping most of the headline features.

It ranks third because it is an older series on a smaller panel, and it matches the C6 on listed features, so there is little listed reason to prefer it other than cost. That is the whole case: if the price gap between a C5 and a C6 is meaningful, the C5 is smart buying.

Buy it for a medium room where you want OLED without paying for the newest series. The caveat is verifying that the price is actually lower on the day, since the bucket is the same as the C6's. Skip it if you want the newest series.

products.name: Samsung 55-Inch Class S90H Series
products.verdict: Samsung's S90H in a smaller 55 inch size.
products.description:
The Samsung S90H in 55 inches is an OLED set in the $500 and up bucket, with the same short listing as its larger siblings. It is Samsung's answer for smaller rooms, built on the same OLED panel family as the 65 and 77 inch versions.

It ranks fourth because the LG C5 offers more listed detail at the same size, including Dolby Atmos. If you do not care about Atmos and prefer Samsung's interface, the gap shrinks, but the listing leaves you with fewer facts to rely on.

It suits bedrooms and compact lounges, especially in Samsung households. Skip it if you want more listed features. As with every S90H listing here, confirm HDMI ports and refresh rate before buying, because neither is stated and both matter to console owners.

products.name: LG 42-Inch Class OLED evo AI 4K C6 Series Smart TV w/Dolby Atmos
products.verdict: The only 42 inch OLED here, for desks and small rooms.
products.description:
The LG 42 inch C6 is an OLED evo 4K set with AI features and Dolby Atmos, in the $500 and up bucket. It is the only compact OLED in the ranking, small enough for a desk, a bedroom shelf or a small apartment wall.

It ranks fifth because few rooms want a 42 inch TV, and the price is premium for a small screen. What you get is the smallest way into the newer C6 series, with the same panel type and audio listing as the 65 inch.

Buy it for a desk or small bedroom where you want OLED black levels in a compact body. Skip it if you sit far from the screen, since 42 inches shrinks quickly at distance. The caveat is paying a large-screen price for a small one. A 55 inch C5 gives more picture for similar money.
products.skipIf: You sit far from the screen.

products.name: Samsung 77-Inch Class S90H Series
products.verdict: A 77 inch OLED for big walls and dedicated viewing rooms.
products.description:
The Samsung 77 inch S90H is the largest OLED in the roundup, in the $500 and up bucket, with the same brief listing as the other S90H models. At this size, the screen becomes the room's centerpiece.

It ranks last because 77 inches suits few rooms and the listing gives little to separate it from the smaller S90H sets. For a large wall it is the only size jump available here, but it asks for a strong mount, a deep seating distance and a large budget.

Buy it for a home theater with a wide wall. Skip it if your wall is under about six feet, or if you sit close. Confirm the weight and VESA pattern on the maker's page before ordering a mount, because none of that appears in the listing, and a wrong bracket is a costly mistake on a wall.

whatMatters.detail: Size depends on viewing distance. Sit about 1.2 to 1.6 times the diagonal away for 4K, and measure the wall and seat distance before choosing. A set that is too large for the room makes the picture feel crowded, and one that is too small leaves detail wasted on a wide wall. Treat the rule as a starting point and sit in your own room.

LG names series like C5 and C6, and the higher number is newer. Newer series may bring updates, while older ones often cost less. Check the model name in the title and compare the same size across years. Prices shift as new models land, so the older set can be the value pick, as long as the discount is real and the warranty matches.

OLED lights each pixel individually, so blacks are deep and contrast is high. Static images shown for very long periods are a known risk, so vary content and avoid leaving a paused screen on. Confirm OLED is named in the listing, since some Mini-LED sets use similar wording in titles and cost less.

Dolby Atmos support is listed on the LG models. It matters if you use a soundbar or an Atmos receiver, since the TV must pass the format through. Look for it in the title, and check the eARC port on the maker's page if you plan to add external speakers.

The Samsung listings here are brief. Check the manufacturer page for ports and refresh rates before buying, because gamers need HDMI 2.1 and a high refresh rate to use a console well. A short listing is a reason to ask questions, not to assume features are included, so do the homework before checkout.

faq.a: OLED panels light each pixel individually, allowing deep blacks and strong contrast. It differs from LED-backlit TVs, where one backlight shines through the panel, and it explains the premium price, because each pixel is its own light source.

Static images shown for very long periods can cause it, so vary content and use screensavers. Normal viewing with the LG C6 or Samsung S90H rarely triggers it, but a paused menu or a game HUD left on for many hours can.

faq.q: Is a C6 worth it over a C5?
faq.a: Only if the price gap is small. The listings show similar headline features, so a C5 at a real discount beats a C6 at full price. Check both prices on the day you buy, and compare return terms, since a deal is only a deal if you can return it.
Choosing size without measuring viewing distance. A 77 inch S90H overwhelms a small room, and a 42 inch C6 shrinks on a long wall. Measure first, then match the panel to the seat and the wall.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Mount or stand it, connect Wi-Fi and your soundbar, then pick a picture mode for your room. The LG models support Dolby Atmos, so route audio through the proper HDMI port for the soundbar, and check the TV's audio output setting.

faq.q: Why did you leave out a few sizes?
faq.a: We dropped duplicate sizes of the same series to keep the roundup varied. The ranking covers the main sizes and brands rather than every variant, so check the lineup page for others.

finalTake: Buy the LG 65 inch C6 for a main living room, or the Samsung S90H if you prefer its interface. The LG C5 55 inch can save money if the price gap is real. Small spaces suit the 42 inch C6, and big walls the 77 inch S90H. Check series year first, then size.
